title: Exact Byte-Level Probabilities from Tokenized Language Models for FIM-Tasks and Model Ensembles

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution aims to characterize and formalize the prediction-time behavioral differences between tokenized LMs and their byte-level equivalents, specifically the 'tokenization bias' phenomenon. Paper [10] ("Understanding and Mitigating Tokenization Bias in Language Models") explicitly investigates tokenization-induced sampling bias and its impact on next-token prediction, aligning closely with the stated purpose. Paper [5] ("Problematic Tokens: Tokenizer Bias in Large Language Models") also traces disparities in model behavior to tokenization processes, but focuses on under-resourced languages rather than general prediction-time behavior. Paper [4] ("A Peek into Token Bias") explores token bias in logical reasoning tasks but does not generalize to the broader statistical equivalence or prediction-time behavior. Thus, [10] is the closest match.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces the Byte-Token Representation Lemma, proving statistical equivalence between byte-level and tokenized models and illustrating tokenization bias via a closed-form Markov chain example. Paper [1] ("Toward a Theory of Tokenization in LLMs") studies transformers trained on simple Markov processes, but does not formalize statistical equivalence or introduce a lemma mapping byte-level and tokenized distributions. Paper [8] ("The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads") uses Markov chains to study in-context learning but does not address tokenization bias or statistical equivalence. Paper [16] ("Markov chain Monte Carlo test of toric homogeneous Markov chains") discusses Markov chains but in a completely unrelated context. No prior paper proves statistical equivalence or introduces a comparable lemma, so the mechanism is uncovered.

### Evaluation
The contribution uses a theoretical evaluation design: definitions, lemmas, and a closed-form Markov chain example illustrating tokenization bias. Paper [1] ("Toward a Theory of Tokenization in LLMs") employs theoretical analysis of transformers on Markov processes, which matches the evaluation design. Paper [8] ("The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads") also uses Markov chains for theoretical analysis, aligning with the evaluation design. Paper [10] ("Understanding and Mitigating Tokenization Bias in Language Models") uses theoretical definitions and examples to analyze tokenization bias, further matching the evaluation design. Thus, the evaluation design is covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of language model tokenization and theory of LLMs. Papers [1], [3], [5], [10], and [11] all address tokenization in the context of language models, covering various aspects such as tokenization bias, subword robustness, and encoding schemes. These works collectively establish language model tokenization as a well-explored domain. Therefore, the domain is covered.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to demonstrate the practical utility of the next-byte method for fill-in-the-middle (FIM) coding tasks and ensembling LMs with distinct vocabularies. No prior paper explicitly establishes the same empirical relationship or utility for the next-byte method in these contexts. While some papers (e.g., [13], [8], [7]) discuss ensembling or heterogeneous mixtures of experts, they do not address the specific utility of next-byte methods for FIM coding or vocabulary ensembling. Similarly, papers like [10] and [9] discuss tokenization issues but do not establish the same purpose of demonstrating next-byte utility for FIM or ensembling.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves applying the next-byte conversion to FIM prompts that terminate mid-token (avoiding out-of-distribution tokenization) and combining predictions of models with different vocabularies in a shared byte space for averaging/mixture-of-experts ensembling. Paper [15] introduces byte-level language models, which operate in a shared byte space, and [13] discusses bridging vocabulary gaps for LLM ensembles, but neither explicitly applies next-byte conversion to FIM prompts or addresses mid-token termination issues. Paper [10] addresses token alignment for subword completion, which is conceptually similar to handling mid-token prompts, but does not use next-byte conversion or byte-space ensembling.

### Evaluation
The evaluation reports improvements on FIM coding benchmarks and ensembles across reasoning, knowledge, and coding baselines. Paper [13] evaluates ensembles of LLMs across diverse baselines, which matches the evaluation design of measuring ensemble performance across tasks. Similarly, [10] evaluates tokenization methods on text completion tasks, which aligns with the evaluation design for FIM coding benchmarks. Both papers use standard benchmark families and metrics, making the evaluation design covered.

### Domain
The domain includes code completion (FIM) and LLM ensembling. Paper [13] explicitly addresses LLM ensembling, and [10] addresses tokenization issues in generative models, which overlap with the domain of FIM coding tasks. Both papers operate in the same general application areas, even if the specific sub-problems differ.
